The proposed concept of branes in the context of gravity is analogous to objecting surfaces within a curved manifold of higher dimensions. Branes can exist across various dimensions and are associated with spaces that have distinct properties, such as the capacity to compress and release energy. Unlike traditional theoretical objects, branes exhibit irreversible behaviors when interacting with each other, which can result in non-reversible changes in their motion. This study aims to illustrate how incorporating time-reversal constraints into braney systems leads to the discovery of new non-reversible symmetries, which can emerge from combining time-reversal and spatial rotation symmetries. A specific mathematical formula representing the energy exchanged between two branes under collision has been developed, demonstrating how the time-reversal constraint can lead to the emergence of a non-reversible force, which is connected to the force of gravity. Furthermore, it is proposed that the energy exchanged between colliding branes could give rise to particle production, which is influenced by the properties of the branes involved and can vary depending on the direction of travel.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in different directions. Notwithstanding the advancements in ultrasound technology, axial and lateral (stretch and slide) tissue displacements are often over/underestimated due to the limited field of view of the scanner, main lobe of the transducer's beam, and sound speed assumptions, respectively. As a result, the virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique has been proposed to handle the lateral displacement challenge. 

However, the VSSA technique suffers from the limited availability of annotated training data for its machine learning-based model, halting its translation to clinical practice. To overcome this hurdle, this research introduces an iterative training approach for the VSSA technique, leveraging only unannotated data.

In experiments conducted on 5 subjects, the proposed method outperformed the conventional technique by 12.5%, and globally optimal models achieved a 1.5-fold improvement in estimation accuracy. 

In contrast to the conventional technique with high sensitivity to sound speed assumptions, the proposed method demonstrated robustness in scenarios with divergent sound speed assumptions.

We introduce a new specification language, Rho, for expressing the essence of algorithms through pseudocode and their underlying logic. This framework bridges the gap between computational systems and logical proofs, enabling the translation of Rho specifications into relevant proofs. In turn, these proofs can be executed as code, achieving full equivalence with the original specifications and demonstrating that this approach produces functional code from proofs. Although initially simple, our system already effectively captures fundamental aspects of recursion and data modification in arrays. Nonetheless, it falls short of addressing issues like concurrency and mutation in data structures.

The concept of Ramsey character was initially developed in relation to graph theory, 
where the focus was on the minimum number of colors required to differentiate between 
two distinct, uniformly distributed sets within a specific graph. Over time, this 
theoretical approach was expanded to other areas, including the Boolean lattices, 
enabling the assessment of Ramsey characteristics for various patterns in these 
lattices. This study aims to determine the Ramsey character of a particular type, 
known as the V-shaped posets, within the Boolean lattices. To achieve this, the 
researchers developed two main methods to find the Ramsey numbers in question. 
Initially, they employed a direct calculation method, while in cases where this 
approach was not feasible, they used a more indirect method that involved breaking 
down the Boolean lattices into smaller components, known as intervals, to 
subsequently identify the relevant Ramsey numbers for these intervals. Furthermore, 
the researchers established upper and lower limits for the Ramsey numbers in 
question, providing a range in which these numbers are likely to fall. Although 
the results of this study are primarily focused on the Boolean lattices, they may 
also be applied to other similar structures: the posets composed of the Boolean 
lattices under the transitive reduction.

In the $k$-centers problem, we are tasked with selecting a subset of $k$ centers that minimizes the maximum distance from any data point to its nearest center. This problem has significant implications in various fields due to its relevance to unsupervised learning and robust optimization. We investigate a dynamic version of the $k$-centers problem, where new data points can be added over time, and we aim to maintain an up-to-date clustering with a dynamic number of centers that adapts to the changing data distribution. Our main contribution is a new algorithm, called DYNAMO, that efficiently solves the dynamic $k$-centers problem for any fixed $k$ by exploiting the properties of high-dimensional data, specifically its association with a fixed $\ell_p$ ball. DYNAMO operates in linear time and maintains an approximate solution using a small set of centers that can be updated on the addition of each new data point. Furthermore, we prove that DYNAMO's performance closely approaches the optimal solution, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through extensive experiments on large-scale datasets, showing a significant improvement over existing methods.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving challenges in solving dynamic, stochastic chaser-evaser games through decomposition. Our approach divides the game into simplified sub-models representing optimal policy behaviors at different level hierarchies. Specifically, we propose a dual-hierarchical structure where the highest level features a basic model that accounts for boundary conditions, and the lowest level includes highly detailed state representations. Our method ensures the lowest level's state space is manageable by incorporating implicit path planning. We demonstrate the efficacy of our hierarchical model by applying it to the solution of a complex maze-solving task, achieving a substantial reduction in computation time. Our research on hierarchical decomposition offers a promising solution for addressing scalability issues in solving challenging stochastic chaser-evaser games.

A likelihood function that fulfills the standard criteria is typically a cyclic and nontransitive measure of the relative plausibility of various models.  However, the term "nontransitive" is actually a misnomer in this context, as it implies the absence of a overarching order.  In contrast, the likelihood ratio test does give a transitive ordering of models by their power to predict data.  It distinguishes more complex models that are themselves nontransitive in their ability to predict data when they have a common parameter and are conditioned on that parameter.  A key aspect of this distinction arises when we consider the ability of a model to predict a specific subset of the data given another specific subset of the data.  It is this ability that determines the power of a model in predicting the original data.  It is interesting to note that the likelihood ratio test's ordering of models does not take into account their freedom from assumptions or their parsimony.  It only considers their ability to predict the data.  It does, however, consider this ability in a more refined manner than simply looking at how well the data is fit.  It refrains from giving excessive weight to very small discrepancies that can be highly influential in the fitting process.  It achieves this refinement by taking account of the standard errors of parameter estimates and their associated degrees of freedom.  It is this refined manner of evaluating models that leads to the use of the F-statistic in this context.  The F-statistic

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in restoring high-quality images from low-dose CT scans without needing matched paired training data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. In response to these issues, we have introduced a new cycleGAN framework based on an adaptive switchable generator, allowing us to take advantage of the strengths of both coordinate-based and batch-based adaptation methods. By adaptively selecting the most effective conversion direction and mixing the reconstructed images with those from batch normalization, our model is able to efficiently utilize both sources of information. We have evaluated our method against other cycleGAN techniques and alternative deep learning restoration techniques, and our results show that it is not only simpler but also more effective at restoring high-quality images from low-dose CT scans.

Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs sharing STSs while moving unrelated dialogs apart during supervised contrastive training. To maximize unlabeled dialogs' potential, it incorporates a self-supervised contrastive loss to refine the learned representations. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven dialog understanding tasks on four datasets without access to vast unlabeled dialog collections. Moreover, it achieves comparable performance to strong baselines that leverage extensive unlabeled data, demonstrating its value in goal-oriented dialog understanding tasks.

This research aims to examine the geometric characteristics of ideal fluid spacetimes under specific compatibility and skew-tangency conditions, leading to the emergence of a linear determinant equation governing the conformal Yamabe operator. By deriving a key identity and associated integral formula, we establish a criteria for the existence of conformal Ricci-Yamabe solitons within this context. Furthermore, various soliton formation and uniqueness results are established, along with a relation to the original spacetime's Ricci-Yamabe problem.

To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halo nuclei, we utilized the angular momentum projection method on wave functions derived from the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in continuum. Our self-consistent approach effectively accounts for interactions between single particle bound states and the continuum across ground and rotational states. For example, we examined rotational states in 61Cu, a distorted halo nucleus, and found that its collective characteristics can be understood through our approach, specifically demonstrating how distortions in halo configurations affect the separation of intrinsic and collective properties.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in NTIRE 2021, earning several top ranks, with codes and models available on MMEditing.

The vector boson approximation is a well-established concept in the analysis of high-energy processes, particularly relevant when considering W and Z boson interactions at sufficient energies. However, the theoretical basis of this approximation has not been extensively evaluated, especially with respect to its dependence on the energy and type of heavy particle involved. In a forthcoming report, we will comprehensively examine the accuracy of this approximation across a broad spectrum of energies and configurations, encompassing both hadronic and leptonic decay modes. This initial submission will focus on a specific scenario involving high-energy muon collisions, with an initial review of the technical aspects of the calculation and a detailed examination of the fractional errors associated with the approximation, as a function of energy and final-state particle momentum.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of modular architectures in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning. By systematically varying task similarity, state
dimensionality, and the number of tasks, our results demonstrate that modular
 architectures significantly outperform a single unified model. Moreover, our
findings reveal that this performance gain is largely due to the reduced
catastrophic interference of sensitivities, a concept we introduce to describe
the decline in performance when a learner is exposed to additional tasks. We
further propose the Multi-Task Value Approximation (MTVA) framework, an
efficacious and efficient way for learning multiple tasks using modular
value functions and a shared sensory encoder. MTVA matches or outperforms the
best task-specific models in our experiments and showcases the benefits of
modular architectures in model-based multi-task reinforcement learning.

The paper provides derivations of Li-Yau and Souplet-Zhang type estimates for the equation $u_t=\Delta_\xi p + \lambda u + A(u)$ in a complete, non-compact metric measure space with compact boundary. Furthermore, the paper includes local gradient estimates for the equation $\Delta_\xi(u^p)+\lambda u + A(u) = 0$ on complete, non-compact manifolds with compact boundary.

We correct outdated statements regarding Kurt Godel's early life, his academic and religious views, and his opinions on the possibility of a machine intelligence surpassing humans. We also clarify confusing or inaccurate details from Godel's biography, derived from previously published information. Additionally, we provide precise explanations for two famous theorems named after Godel, along with a discussion on his influence and a brief overview of his personal and professional accomplishments.

This paper formulates the three balls conjecture in terms of monogenic functions, which are essentially the complex extensions of harmonic functions, within the context of Clifford analysis. We then demonstrate the validity of the three balls conjecture for specific functions that are associated with the right regularization of the Poisson kernel. Additionally, the paper establishes upper bounds for the first positive eigenvalue of the Dirac operator, denoted as $\Lambda_1$, which applies generally to functions within the Sobolev space $H^{0, p}$, for $1 < p \leq \infty$. Specifically, we derive the following inequalities: $\Lambda_1 \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} p_s^{(1/p)} |B_1|^{1/p}$, with $p_s$ representing the space $L^{p*}$, and $|B_1|$ denoting the volume of the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^3$. It's also demonstrated that $\Lambda_1 \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, with the note that this result holds equivalently for the left regularization of the Poisson kernel.

The rise of mobile devices and the growing capacity for data storage have enabled the collection of geotagged images on a massive scale.  Despite the wealth of information available from such datasets known as visual landcovers, they have not been consistently matched with ground truths across different regions.  The lack of uniformity in such datasets in particular equities poses a significant challenge in applying machine learning models to them.  In this research, a novel approach to sequence-based sampling was presented that maintains the equilibrium of visual landcover datasets.  The proposed method called SEQSAM successfully achieves this by combining two complementary sampling techniques.  In experiments conducted with datasets collected from Google Street View, SEQSAM demonstrated its effectiveness in maintaining the balance of datasets by comparing its performance to two alternative methods.  Furthermore, SEQSAM's effectiveness was validated in a pilot application involving the classification of aerial images using deep learning models.

To facilitate versatile visual manipulation tasks, eye-in-hand camera calibration is crucial for obtaining precise positional and rotational data. Unlike other camera calibration methods that rely on external signals, image-based calibration can be fully automated. However, the process is challenging due to the complex relationships between image coordinates and camera parameters in 6DoF space. This paper introduces an innovative algorithm to calibrate the camera within a grasped object, within a 6DoF space, using a single image. The method leverages deep learning techniques to predict missing image features, infer object orientation, and ultimately solve for camera parameters through linear algebra. Experimental results show that our proposed system can accurately calculate camera parameters with minimal training, outperforming traditional optimization-based methods.

In various applications, researchers face the challenge of solving inverse problems, which involve recovering a physical quantity of interest from noisy and limited-range measurements. Due to the ill-posed nature of these problems, accurate reconstruction is necessary to interpret scientific data effectively. For such purposes, we introduce a novel regularization technique for conditional generative adversarial networks, which incorporates a data-driven prior to facilitate posterior estimation. By utilizing a realized MCMC sample set as training data, our approach bypasses the computational expense associated with simultaneous reconstruction and inverse problems. Through numerical experiments in optical imaging and seismic uncertainty quantification, our proposed framework demonstrates superior performance compared to traditional methods.

This article examines the concept of locally invariant surfaces in fractional dynamical systems near equilibria. By extending classical methods, we develop a novel approach using the Gamma-capacity to demonstrate that in sufficiently high-dimensional spaces, a significant class of nonlinear, smooth surfaces fails to maintain invariance. This generalizes previous results from integer-order systems to fractional order systems.

Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that could be achieved by utilizing Terahertz communications, which can provide very high bandwidths. Nevertheless, THz communications' relatively short signal transmission distance necessitates the use of multi-hop transmissions to cover longer distances. Nevertheless, traditional optimization techniques often overlook a critical aspect of these systems: the time-efficient acquisition of high-gain directional links during beam training, which can result in a significant delay. This difficulty becomes more pronounced in scenarios like autonomous vehicular networks where rapid beam training is essential. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel machine-learning-based approach that efficiently identifies optimal activating links within a limited time frame. By utilizing this approach in an online learning environment, we develop an iterative algorithm capable of effectively determining the optimal set of links to activate in each time slot, thus maximizing the overall beam training efficiency. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate that our proposed technique can yield a substantial increase in beam training speed, outperforming even traditional optimization methods by up to 90%.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs away from the Sun and is moving at a galactic longitude similar to that of the Sun, with only a slight difference in velocity. This screen's orientation is perpendicular to the line of sight to the pulsar. It takes approximately 11.5 years for this screen to complete one orbital cycle around the Sun. The discovery of screens like this one has the potential to significantly impact our understanding of the interstellar medium, allowing for the study of long-lived structures and how they interact with the Sun and surrounding space.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent expanded convolutional neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with a generative network architecture that incorporates a Pitch-dependent Expanded Convolution Neural Network. The model exploits the non-negative relationship between pitch and spectral characteristics to facilitate generalizability. Through the extension of convolution layers for temporal and spectral signal exploration, QPNet is expected to improve WaveNet's pitch control performance. Experimental evaluations conducted on speech and instrument audio demonstrated the superior pitch control capabilities of the proposed Quasi-Periodic WaveNet.

This research presents a novel annotation and correction tool for Arabic texts,
namely MADARi, catering to Standard and Dialectal varieties. MADARi offers a
user-friendly interface and efficient management capabilities for annotating and
handling large-scale datasets. Its key features encompass a range of morphological
annotations, such as identifying the base form of words, associated prepositions,
and grammatical components like nominative and accusative markers. Additionally,
MADARi addresses the issue of incorrect spelling present in many Arabic corpora.
To demonstrate its effectiveness, the project incorporates a set of morphological
rules and a spell-checking engine, leveraging the MFRA Corpus's annotated data
to fine-tune its performance through a web-based interface.

As exoplanets with manageable temperatures and sizable atmospheres are discovered at an increasing rate, it's essential to understand how these planets interact with their starlight. Existing strategies for analyzing these planets are typically based on highly simplified models of atmospheres, which may not accurately capture crucial details, especially if the atmospheres contain unknown gas species that can affect their phaseoltical properties. Using a advanced modeling approach, this study simulates and analyzes the spectral patterns of various gas species in exoplanet atmospheres as they interact with different types of stars. By considering multiple atmospheric conditions and gas species, researchers can proceed with caution in drawing conclusions about the atmospheric composition of exoplanets based on their photochemical features. In doing so, this study paves the way for a more comprehensive understanding of temperate exoplanets and their analytical characterization.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves a unique perspective that focuses on tunneling spectroscopy with high Ohmic resistance in voltage-biased setups, particularly using resistive electrodes. These setups, characterized by large resistance (between the sample and the measurement device), cause significant electrical losses that effectively hinder the usual distinction between Majorana and other peaks based on the sample's spin state. However, this technique requires a theoretical understanding of tunneling spectra in voltage-biased setups that account for Ohmic dissipation, a phenomenon that has not been thoroughly studied in tunneling spectroscopy. Therefore, we have developed a comprehensive approach to analyze tunneling spectra in voltage-biased setups, and our results indicate that it is possible to differentiate between Majorana and other causes based on the shape of the tunneling spectrum at non-zero temperatures.

The development of advanced detection algorithms through deep learning has accelerated the efficient identification of road defects. Nonetheless, implementing these advancements across entire transportation networks poses significant challenges due to the need for constant vehicle patrols and extensive visual inspections. To address this, we've developed a pioneering approach, called RoadAtlas, which utilizes unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to rapidly pinpoint potential road flaws across broad areas. This system combines cutting-edge deep learning technology with spatial reasoning to minimize the false negative rate and reduce the burden of subsequent ground validations. Additionally, RoadAtlas leverages geographic information to determine the most effective inspection route for each detected issue, optimizing road flaw prioritization and asset management. We've tested and refined this innovative system using a dataset from the Texas Department of Transportation, and our results demonstrate its efficacy in identifying a wide range of road defects and optimizing inspection workflows.

The concept of shadows constitutes a broad generalization of the idea of edges in oriented surfaces. We undertake a fundamental exploration of shadows, mapping the natural bicategorical framework of shadows to the realm of oriented surfaces and their associated graph-computing structures. Through this investigation, we arrive at an abstract definition of shadows that reflects their intrinsic properties, thereby enabling a direct extension to three-dimensional pleated surfaces through a system of graph-computing structures inspired by Spencer Thomas's work. This three-dimensional generalization, in turn, paves the way for a definition of shadowy maps between pleated surfaces.

Our research aims to address the challenging task of identifying noisy images that are mislabeled in a dataset, with the ultimate goal of preventing the learning of misleading features. During the training of deep learning models, redundant or misleading visual information can often mask essential context, hindering progress in object recognition tasks. We propose a novel evaluation framework that assesses a dataset's cleanliness by testing the ability of state-of-the-art object recognition models to accurately classify noisy images. Our findings reveal that existing evaluation frameworks fall short in validating the reliability of datasets. To address this issue, we introduce the CleanNet-Benchmark, consisting of the CleanNet dataset, which is renowned for its high data quality, along with corresponding class labels. Our analysis demonstrates that modern object recognition models are susceptible to noisy suprabilities, with poor performance on certain classes that are heavily influenced by visual artifacts. We devise the CleanNet-Benchmark score, a comprehensive score that evaluates the robustness of a dataset by assessing a model's precision in classifying clean images and estimating the prevalence of clean images across all classes. According to our calculations, the CleanNet-Benchmark score ranks the CleanNet dataset as the most robust, followed by the ImageNet and SVHN datasets. In contrast, the recently introduced TSS dataset underperforms due to its relatively poor cleanliness. We anticipate that the CleanNet-Benchmark score will guide researchers in developing more resilient evaluation frameworks and enhancing the cleanliness of visual datasets.

Current Graph Neural Networks, based on Euclidean space, have a significant limitation
in handling distant nodes. This restriction originates from the impractical assumption
that node connections only extend a finite number of steps. Real-world applications,
such as social networks and molecular structures, often involve long-range relationships.
Existing methods fall into two inadequate categories to address this challenge: some try
to circumvent it by shortening distances, while others fail to provide a theoretical basis.
We propose a novel Labeled Graph Neural Network framework that overcomes this limitation
by incorporating a Lorentzian metric. This metric allows nodes with significantly
different properties to be connected, enabling robust multi-task learning without
restricting the extent of node connections. Formulated within a fixed metric space,
our approach avoids the need to readjust the metric during training. We demonstrate
the effectiveness of our method by conducting extensive experiments on various datasets
and achieving superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art GNNs.

This study seeks to contradict a well-known challenge in partial differential equation (PDE) inverse problems. Generally, the solution's spatial distribution cannot be determined instantaneously, given the PDE in question. However, this research demonstrates that for specific coupled PDEs, determining the structure's distribution can be achieved through an initial shock wave using only spatial information. This method involves solving a global problem to obtain the desired structure. Interestingly, the technique can also recover non-unique structures corresponding to distinct acoustic signal arrival times. Additionally, this approach is shown to be robust with regard to additional smooth components. Nonetheless, it fails when the structure's characteristics are changeable.

A new method has been proposed to achieve the steady-state compression of quantum fields through the interaction of optical and mechanical modes. A unitary transformation was utilized to transfer the energy from the optical mode to the mechanical mode at a set rate. This transformation is part of a larger quartic interaction and was found using a quantum circuit model. As a result, a family of equivalent transformations was identified that all result in the same outcome of transferring energy. Furthermore, this method was shown to be resistant to decoherence in the optical mode. A second scheme was also proposed that uses a different unitary transformation to achieve the same outcome of energy transfer. This scheme relies on an interplay between driving fields in both the optical and mechanical modes. It was found that in the steady state, energy is transferred from the optical mode to the mechanical mode, with the amount of energy transferred depending on the driving field strengths. This process is also resistant to decoherence in the optical mode.

We examine an expansion of modal $\mu$-calculus, specifically considering its application to first-order logic with equality and disjoint unions of tuples. This expanded version, which we call $\mu$E, maintains the basic properties of modal $\mu$-calculi while incorporating the capabilities of first-order logic. $\mu$E displays more intricate behavioral patterns compared to the restricted modal $\mu$-calculi, such as independence from arithmetical interpretations and limited expressiveness compared to modal $\mu$-calculi with path formulas. Nonetheless, $\mu$E possesses decidability in its basic form and an optimal exponential complexity for model checking, and it achieves this through a contraction of possible models that originates from the restrictions of tuples and equalsities. Additionally, $\mu$E exhibits better model checking performance than the combination of modal $\mu$-calculi with strong background logic, and it facilitates the expression of patterns that are inherently multi-modal yet still retain the simplicity of modal $\mu$-calculi.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
psychological context.

In this research, we explore how Hefty Gravity's new gauge symmetry, related to harmonic functions, affects the general form of a static, spherically symmetric metric. By applying a specific transformation to the metric, we can bring it into a form that aligns with Hefty Gravity's gauge, without resorting to specific coordinate transformations. This new perspective reveals that both the metric and associated gauge vectors can be expressed through the use of Jacobi elliptic functions, indicating that Hefty Gravity's predictions outperform General Relativity in certain scenarios due to increased flexibility in metric configurations.

A signed graph is created by adding a polarity to the edges of an existing graph, and this concept of signed graphs has recently been integrated with other graph theory ideas like minors and coloring. By examining the notion of polarity, researchers have discovered that certain inequalities involving the number of edges in a graph are affected by whether the edges are polarized in a certain direction. This paper explores how the number of edges in a graph is related to its chromatic number when a specific type of polarization is applied, and it identifies an upper limit for the number of edges in a graph that will guarantee a certain chromatic number when a particular type of polarization is used. This guarantee comes in the form of a condition involving the graph's minor, and it creates a new upper limit for certain families of graphs like planar graphs. Additionally, this paper discusses how this concept of polarization can be applied to other areas of graph theory, like the four-color theorem, and it introduces the idea of expanded double covers as a way to study the properties of polarized graphs.

In the Weyl-Wigner representation, phase space and classical mechanics are overlaid to form the Wigner function, which serves as a canonical distribution. However, this representation encounters difficulties when attempting to directly link classical mechanics and quantum mechanics through the Weyl-Wigner transform. A novel approach has been developed to address these challenges, allowing for the analysis of canonical equilibrium states within the Weyl-Wigner representation. By demonstrating that these states conform to a generalized form, investigators have identified key conditions underling their formulation. Furthermore, this framework is shown to encompass multiple variants of the Wigner function, including those resulting from the Weyl-Wigner transformation of pure Gaussian states and those represented through the Garside monoid. A distinctive characteristic of these states is the presence of an invariant standard basis, which is derived from the Weyl-Wigner matrix and is linked to the symplectic metriples. Finally, this work is expected to provide a definitive answer to the question of what constitutes the Weyl-Wigner representation of canonical equilibrium states.

The concept of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical idea. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature.

Let G be an additive group of integers, and S a nonempty subset of G. For any positive integer k, we define the restricted signed sumset of S to be the set of integers obtained by adding up k elements of S, where the signs are chosen from the set {-1,1}. Let A be the smallest positive integer for which the restricted signed sumset of S satisfies the inequality |x| ≤ A^k. It is known that A is bounded by 2k times the largest prime factor of S. Here we show that every integer less than or equal to (sqrt(2)-1)sqrt{k} can be represented as the restricted signed sum of two subsets of S.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to determine patient risk and appropriate treatment. However, accurate diagnosis through histological analysis alone can be complicated for non-experts and requires further investigation for validation. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, a comprehensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated images detailing colorectal polyp morphology. These images are extracted from whole-slide scans, organized into three categories based on polyp type and two levels based on adenoma severity. Furthermore, we've demonstrated the difficulty of colorectal polyp classification and grading through a simple baseline model. To improve classification performance, we've refined a segmentation module within the backbone network, achieving a 6% improvement in accuracy. For grading, a more complex approach was effective in distinguishing mild and severe adenomas but struggled with middle-stage adenoma classification. UniToPatho is an open-source dataset available for further research advancement.

A novel numerical strategy has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered around analyzing the impact of smoothly varying material inhomogeneities on plane waves. This strategy leverages the Fourier-BEM and a fixed mesh, and adapts to both very soft and very hard inclusions relative to the surrounding medium. Two main features of this method are a highly efficient way of computing bounded difference between the actual and plane wave solutions using a finite element approach, and a specialized algebraic solver for inverse problems. Another key aspect is the implementation of an adaptive technique for reconstructing coefficient variations, which can be applied to both smooth and discontinuous variations. However, it should be noted that only plane wave references are used in this analysis.

We analyzed the isotopic composition of oxygen, calcium-aluminum-rich meteorites from the Chelyabinsk and Benenitra falls with distinct analytical results. Due to the use of different techniques, combining chelyabinsk and benenitra data required significant scrutiny. However, when the information was reconciled, we discovered a previously unseen disparity in isotopic values in the two groups. This variation may indicate varying isotopic content in different planetesimals within the inner solar system that accreted into the same asteroid parent body. In order to explain these findings, we had to revise our current understanding of how partially melted planetesimals release oxygen isotopic fractionation. If our hypothesis is correct, then this would provide further evidence that damp or cold accretion played a significant role in forming the inner solar system's planetesimals.

Using the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method, we find exact expressions for scalar products and form factors of higher-spin XXZ lattices, reproducing known results for spinless systems and generalizing them for finite lattices. By examining these results, we identify a representation of the affine quantum group $U_q(\hat{sl_2})$ within the XXZ model's imaginary-frequency domain. This finding allows us to derive explicit, monodromy-agnostic formulas for form factors and scalar products. By consolidating previous findings and ours, the finite-lattice XXZ model's imaginary-frequency domain is shown to be consistently described by the affine quantum group $U_q(\hat{sl_2})$.

Translation between languages has long been a fundamental challenge addressed by machine learning methods. Suppose we have two distinct languages, A and B. In typical scenarios, training two separate models on data from languages A and B would be necessary to facilitate translation between these languages. This approach however, is impractical when dealing with multiple languages as it requires extensive retraining. In such cases, training a single model that can translate between any pair of languages despite never having seen those specific languages during training would be highly desirable. This paper takes the first step in achieving this goal for voice translations by demonstrating the feasibility of translating from English into other languages without any additional training on those specific languages. It accomplishes this by utilizing a single neural network model that can handle both text and voice inputs and leverages token-based attention to focus on the most relevant characters within each input. In our experiments, this approach shows promising results in translating English to other languages with accuracy outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in zero-shot settings.

We assess the applicability of three different methods for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, irreducible multipoles and spherical multipoles. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated using an array of examples spanning from gas-phase atoms and molecules to solid particles, encompassing isolated systems and interactions between particles. Furthermore, we demonstrate that spherical multipoles can capture the optical force experienced by particles when placed within an external electromagnetic field.

This study introduces two concepts, quantum immanents and double Young-Capelli bitableaux, which are closely intertwined, and a third concept, Schur shifted symmetric expressions, that is closely related to the former two. Specifically, this research demonstrates that certain elements of the full centralizer of the irreducible Schur shifted symmetric representations of the quantum general linear group u_q(gl_n) act as double Young-Capelli bitableaux, and correspondingly, their product with a specific element of the Weyl group W_0 (i.e., the element s_{n-1}...s_1) yields a quantum immanent. Conversely, any quantum immanent can be expressed as the product of W_0 with a double Young-Capelli bitableaux. This relationship enables the computation of individual basis components of the irreducible Schur shifted symmetric representations through the use of the classical limit procedure. Ultimately, this is shown to result in a novel, straightforward formula for calculating specific elements of the representation, such as its character or Weyl group action, in a particular limit. This, in turn, allows for a more direct understanding of the representations themselves.

Within the context of the easiest scoto-seesaw model, we have coupled the 54-dimensional neutrino space with two right-handed neutrino singlets to formulate a minimalistic framework that incorporates dark matter within the simplest form of the scalar sector. By integrating this model into the most fundamental version of the standard model, we have introduced new contributions to the running of the standard model parameters, specifically beta functions for the neutrino mass, dark matter mass, and a newly created aqueous-terreous parameter. Furthermore, we have observed that the ease with which this model accommodates dark matter coexistence with neutrinos relies heavily on the inherent properties of the neutrino sector, including the ironical control of the neutrino mass deficit by the dark matter mass. Meanwhile, we have discovered that the Higgs vacuum stability is influenced by the dark sector's minimal nature, resulting in a relatively high threshold for instability, positioned at approximately $\mathcal{O}(10^{10})$ GeV. Nonetheless, we have found that the most critical aspect influencing the dark matter stability is the dark matter self-coupling parameter, $\lambda_{\rm DM}/\Lambda^3$, which must exceed $\sim 10^{-10}$ to ensure $10^{\rm o}$ of a lifetime as long as $10^{26}$ years for the dark matter to remain stable. Ultimately, we have established that the most demanding condition for this model is the achievement of neutrino mass at below $10

We employ first-principles calculations to investigate the electronic structure of transition metal oxides, focusing on the separation between $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ molecular orbitals. Our analysis reveals that this separation is not as sharp as commonly assumed and is instead influenced by both spin-orbit and crystal field effects. As a result, we demonstrate that a simple model, incorporating these interactions, can accurately describe the split states, thereby bypassing the need for more complex multiplet simulations. Utilizing this model, we explore how the spin-orbit interaction affects charge, orbital, and spin dynamics within these materials. Furthermore, we show that increasing the size of the $d$-orbital enhances the distinction between $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ states while broadening the $e_g$ peak in spectroscopic analyses.

Quantum field theories, typically used for describing physical systems, also have applications in mathematical concepts of algebraic geometry. Through a process called quantum localization, these theories transform into precise geometric objects, related to the algebraic variety and its symplectic deformation. When varying the variety, either by changing parameters or using a technique called birational transformation, the corresponding quantum field theory also changes. However, the relationship between these variations is not directly understood. In this research, we focus on local, smooth transformations of varieties and identify a well-defined theory, called relative quantum field theory, that captures the variations of quantum field theories through algebraic geometry's geometric invariant, specifically the symplectic structure. We demonstrate that this approach is independent of the specific transformation used and is instead determined by the variety's structure. As a result, we can predict the properties of the relative quantum field theories, including their symplectic structure and the associated geometric operators, for any variety obtained from a transformation. Furthermore, we show that this approach applies to varieties with singular points and can be generalized to involve change in parameters through a process called geometric invariant theory.

Doctors and non-experts alike, rely heavily on visual cues when interpreting medical images, including chest X-rays. These interpretations are often influenced by the presentation format of images. Current studies focusing on medical imaging typically disregard the processing history, which includes adjustments made during the filming process and subsequent editing of radiographs. However, processing decisions, such as contrast and brightness levels, can significantly impact physicians' diagnoses. In our research, we investigate the effect of radiograph processing on medical specialists' interpretations. To achieve this, we developed an analysis framework, which pinpointed key processing parameters influencing physicians' assessments. Utilizing this insight, we established guidelines for producing high-quality, uniformly processed chest X-rays. These guidelines form the foundation for our proposed editing protocol, which aims to prevent the re-introduction of processing biases when digitally manipulating medical images.

ViDaExpert is an intuitive data visualization and advanced statistical tool for users from various disciplines who need to work with multidimensional Euclidean space data that contains symbolic information associated with samples and variables. It provides a user-friendly interface linked to a powerful statistical engine, enabling the exploration of data structures through methods like PCA, multidimensional scattering, and UMAP, as well as custom transformations and specialized visualizations such as dimensionality discs and spectral emboxes. With its capabilities, ViDaExpert enables users to create customized views and uncover complex data relationships by navigating through interactive 3D visualizations.

Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for many space-time applications, particularly in the analysis of gravitational waves. When using a grid-based approach, a small change in one dimension can lead to a substantial computational cost. Optimizing code Performance is essential for both real-time and post-merger analysis. By employing an FFT-based Nystrom method, we enhance computational efficiency by approximately $O(N)$ when using $N$ particles, regardless of the level of geometric complexity. This is because this method calculates the interaction between particles in $O(N)$ time, in contrast to a direct sum that would take $O(N^2)$. Furthermore, this algorithm can be up to 10 times faster than a direct sum over an irregular domain.
